1:
The embassy from Tyre is philology to one voice, a lesson in dependence to another. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the Hebrew text of Chronicles spells the name Hiram, as do the Septuagint and all other ancient versions of both books, though the Hebrew margin here writes Huram; that messengers means ambassadors; that the cedar was felled in Lebanon and sea-borne to Joppa; and that the craftsmen are literally craftsmen of walls and craftsmen of timber, where Samuel has craftsmen of wood and craftsmen of stone of wall. The house, he insists, is a palace, the Temple being called the house as well as the palace; and he sets the project beside the records of palace building the Assyrian and Babylonian sovereigns left, cedar of Lebanon being a favourite material with them. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws another point from the same transaction: no man is of such sufficiency in himself that he has no need of his neighbours, for David had a very large kingdom and Hiram a very little one, yet David could not build himself a house to his mind unless Hiram furnished workmen and materials, a reason why we should despise none but be obliging to all.

That David perceived the kingdom confirmed is pressed three ways. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) mark the difference from the older text: where Samuel says Jehovah had lifted up his kingdom, the Chronicle says his kingdom had been lifted up on high, the unusual form being probably a passive by contraction, and the phrase on high being here, as often in these books, a way of intensifying the expression. Ellicott renders it that David knew Jehovah had appointed him, and finds the evidence in the embassy itself, the willing alliance of the powerful sovereign of Tyre being so understood by David; the favour of man, he adds, is sometimes a sign of the approval of God, and always so when it results from well-doing. Henry turns it into two maxims. It is a satisfaction to a wise man to be settled, and to a good man to see the special providences of God in his settlement, for the people had made David king but he could not be easy till he perceived that the Lord had confirmed him: who shall unfix me, Henry asks, if God hath fixed me? And we must look on all our advancements as designed for usefulness, since the kingdom was lifted up not that David might look great but because of his people Israel, that he might be their guide and protector: we are blessed in order that we may be blessings.

On the wives and sons they divide between comparison, arithmetic and reproof. Ellicott observes that the verse is considerably abbreviated against Samuel, which reads concubines and wives from Jerusalem after he had come from Hebron, and that the concubines are not omitted out of delicacy, since they are named elsewhere in this book; the list, he says, is repeated because it stood at this point in the document the historian copied, and perhaps as an instance of the prosperity which is the section’s topic; and he notes that Joseph traced his descent from one of these sons. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) counts the names: in Samuel only eleven persons are named in the Hebrew, the Septuagint there has twenty-four, and here there are thirteen, all the versions agreeing in that number with varieties in the names. Henry allows the fault, then the blessing: it is difficult to thrive without growing secure and indulgent to the flesh, and it was David’s infirmity that on settling in his kingdom he took more wives, yet the numerous issue added to his honour and strength, for children are a heritage of the Lord; the account is given here again because it was their honour to have such a father.
7:
The invasion is placed by one voice and moralised by the other. For Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) the word all, which Samuel omits, contrasts David’s second election with his first as king of Judah only; to seek David means with hostile intent; and where our text has he went out against them, literally before them, Samuel has he went down to the stronghold, a term used both of the castle of Zion and of David’s old refuge at Adullam in the valley of Elah. The latter is probably intended, since the Philistines were likely to take the route through that valley, so that David went down from Zion to meet them there; and the narrative then turns back, the invaders having come by another road than usual and encamped in the valley of Rephaim. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the attack as a warning: it forbids us to be secure in any settlement and engages us to expect molestation in this world, for when we are most easy something may come to be a terror to us, and so Christ’s kingdom is insulted by the serpent’s seed, especially when it advances.

How David enquired is answered with precision. Ellicott asks the question directly and answers it: through the high priest Abiathar, who sought divine direction by the Urim and Thummim, or sacred lots, carried in a pouch on his breast fastened to the ephod. He adds a point of punctuation with consequences: there should be a comma and not a query after the word Philistines, the whole sentence forming one question in the Hebrew, where Samuel gives two distinct questions. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supplies the Targum’s rendering: David consulted the Word of the Lord. Henry draws the rule, that David’s enquiring of God once and again should direct us in all our ways to acknowledge him: in distress to fly to him, when wronged to appeal to him, and when we know not what to do to ask counsel at his oracles and beg him to show us the right way.

At Baal-perazim the interest is topographical and verbal. Ellicott notes that it was David and his troops who came up, where Samuel has David alone come into the place; that the locality is unknown; and that Isaiah refers to these two victories together. True to his character, he says, David owns the mighty hand of God in the results of his own valour, conscious of being God’s instrument, which Ellicott contrasts with the haughty self-confidence of the Assyrian conqueror. The image of the breaking forth of waters he takes from the ground, David’s forces having probably charged down the slopes like a mountain torrent. The name itself he renders lord or owner of breaches, adding that the plural may also have meant the fissures on the mountain-side, and that where Samuel has one called the name, our text has they called, indicating the narrative’s antiquity. Clarke again gives the Targum: the Lord had broken the enemies of David like the breaking of a potter’s vessel full of water. Henry makes the victory an encouragement to resist our spiritual enemies in observance of divine direction and dependence on divine strength, the devil resisted fleeing as the Philistines fled.

The burning of the abandoned gods is read as obedience and example. Ellicott observes that where Samuel has images our word is explanatory, and that where Samuel says David and his men carried them off the chronicler says David gave a commandment and they were burned with fire; the two are not incompatible and may both have stood in the same original text, and the chronicler is careful to record David’s compliance with the law in Deuteronomy. Henry takes it as instruction: David’s burning the gods of the Philistines when they fell into his hands should teach us a holy indignation against idolatry and all its remains.
13:
The second enquiry and the manoeuvre it produced come almost entirely from the text. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds the first half of the verse fuller and clearer here than in Samuel, but holds the second half must be adjusted by the older account, which reads: thou must not go up; go round to their rear, and come upon them in front of the baca trees. Probably, he says, the terms rendered after them and from them should be modified and transposed, giving go not up against them, go round to their rear, as Samuel has it. The mulberry trees he calls the traditional Jewish rendering of a Hebrew word that occurs only here and in the parallel passage, and takes them rather for the kind of balsam tree the Arabs call baca, which sheds a gum like tears, whence its name.

What the sound in the tree-tops was divides the two voices sharply. Ellicott renders it the sound of marching and allows that the sign may have been natural, David listening for the wind rustling in the tops of the bacas, a noise like walking on dead leaves, and then making his attack. He grants at once that all ancient peoples attached a prophetic import to the rustling of leaves: omens from trees appear in the great Assyrian work on terrestrial omens compiled by order of Sargon, and in the speaking oaks of Dodona, the laurel of Delos and that of Delphi, the oak of the diviners, perhaps the palm-tree of Deborah, and even the burning bush; the Arabs still believe certain thorny bushes can utter prophetic words. These analogies, he insists, do not militate against the reality or the miraculous character of the occurrence, since divine communications always take the form best adapted for striking the mind amidst reigning ideas, as the visions of Joseph are Egyptian and those of Ezekiel Assyrian. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) leaves nature out and gives the Targum: when thou shalt hear the sound of the angels coming to thy assistance, then go out to battle, for an angel is sent from the presence of God to render thy way prosperous.

The pursuit and the closing reflection raise a question of text and one of scope. Ellicott notes that the present Hebrew of Samuel has Geba while the Septuagint agrees with Chronicles in reading Gibeon, though the Targum and Syriac and Arabic read Geba; he prefers Gibeon, which lay some six miles north-west of Jerusalem between the valley of Rephaim and Gezer, and finds Isaiah in support. The last verse, he adds, is not in Samuel at all and looks like a concluding reflection of the chronicler’s; the fear of David was, as we should say, the natural effect of his victories, though in the chronicler’s view his success in arms, with all its consequences, was the work of Jehovah. Clarke narrows the reach of the fame, that into all lands means all the surrounding or neighbouring lands and nations, for no others can possibly be intended.
